title: A tithe-roll scraped clean for one wrong stroke
summary: Tormod Beag, a copying clerk of Sliochd Thormoid at Seann Dunn, scrapes clean a province's tithe-roll his young son Gilleasbuig has copied with a single stroke too many in it, and makes the boy write the whole roll again from the beginning rather than mend the one line, so that he learns early a mistake quietly mended teaches a clerk less than a roll done wholly over.

title: Oighrig nic Lachlainn's word to a clerk's son
summary: A young Gilleasbuig, carrying his father's rolls to Cathair dhearg at sixteen, is asked by Oighrig nic Lachlainn whose son he is; told his father's name, she says only that the hand is known to her, the one exchange of the whole reign between the woman who holds An Talla Dearg and the clerk who will one day fill it.

title: The clerks keep the shut hall's tallies
summary: Gilleasbuig Mòr, sent down from Seann Dunn the winter after Oighrig nic Lachlainn's death, spends a season sealing rolls and answering reeves at the shut red hall who no longer know whose name to render account to, keeping every tally true on the plain reasoning that whoever fills the hall next will want them so.

title: Gilleasbuig watches Na Ceithir Taighean argue
summary: Called down from Cathair dhearg twice a year to lay the shut hall's own rolls before whichever house asks to see them, Gilleasbuig Mòr sits at the edge of Na Ceithir Taighean' long sitting at Dùn ìseal, and hears blood, boats and silence argued past each other for three years without once being asked his own mind on the matter.

title: Sliochd Raghnaill first names the clerk of the shut hall
summary: Sliochd Raghnaill is the first of Na Ceithir Taighean to put Gilleasbuig Mòr's own name forward for An Talla Dearg, on the reasoning that a clerk who kept the shut hall's rolls straight three years running, favouring no house's claim over the work, has already shown the hand a red hall wants at its head.

title: The line drawn beneath a queen's name
summary: In the year after the cup is set in his hands, Gilleasbuig Mòr has Clàr nan Rìghrean copied again from its beginning in his own house's hand, with a single line drawn beneath the name of Oighrig nic Lachlainn to mark the ending of Goraidh Mòr's whole line, so that no clerk after him need hunt a kinship no longer there.

title: Tormod mac Gilleasbuig sits at the rolls
summary: Gilleasbuig Mòr sends for his son Tormod, already taught the clerks' bench at Seann Dunn at sixteen, to sit beside him at Cathair dhearg and learn An Talla Dearg's own rolls before he is taught anything else of ruling, the same order his own father once taught him a road in.

title: The meadow of Muileann àrsaidh and Ceann àrsaidh
summary: Gilleasbuig Mòr judges the one dispute of his reign the rolls set down whole, a water-meadow claimed whole by two households on notched sticks that agree for forty years and then part company; he sends a clerk to copy both sticks stroke for stroke and gives the meadow to both households at once, with a boundary stone cut down its centre for the first time in living memory.

title: Gilleasbuig Mòr carried five days to Dùn dhearg
summary: Gilleasbuig Mòr's bier is carried the five days' road from Cathair dhearg to Dùn dhearg, stopping each night at a waypoint house whose keeper had known him first as a boy with a satchel of rolls, to be buried among Sliochd Ìomhair as Sliochd Ìomhair had sworn at his choosing.
